parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Dye **H** is very stable because:
> 
> - Delocalised electrons in the π bonding systems of the two benzene rings **[1 mark]**
> - The delocalisation is extended through the -N=N- group, which acts as a bridge between the two rings **[1 mark]**

> Azo dyes contain two arene rings connected by the -N=N- (azo) group.
> 
> The π electrons are delocalised across both benzene rings and the azo bridge, spreading the electron density over the entire conjugated system.
> 
> This extended delocalisation makes the molecule very stable, as the energy is distributed over a larger area rather than being confined to individual bonds.

step 1 ...................................................

step 2 ...................................................

step 3 ...................................................

step 4 ...................................................
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagents and conditions for each step are:
> 
> - Step 1: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCl and AlCl<sub>3</sub> / CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub> and AlCl<sub>3</sub> / heat **[1 mark]**
> - Step 2: CH<sub>3</sub>COCl and AlCl<sub>3</sub> / heat **[1 mark]**
> - Step 3: NaOH and I<sub>2</sub> / Cl<sub>2</sub> / Br<sub>2</sub>, then H<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Step 4: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> in dry ether **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Steps 1 and 2 both involve Friedel-Crafts electrophilic substitution of the benzene ring.
> 
> Step 1 adds an isopropyl group (alkylation). A halogen carrier catalyst such as AlCl<sub>3</sub> is needed to generate the carbocation electrophile:
> 
> AlCl<sub>3</sub> + (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCl → AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> + (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH<sup>+</sup>
>

> 
> AlCl<sub>3</sub> + CH<sub>3</sub>COCl → AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> + CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup>
> 
> Step 3 converts the methyl ketone to a carboxylic acid via the haloform (iodoform) reaction:
> 
> R-CO-CH<sub>3</sub> + 3I<sub>2</sub> + 4OH<sup>-</sup> → CHI<sub>3</sub> + RCOO<sup>-</sup> + 3I<sup>-</sup> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O
> 
> The carboxylate RCOO<sup>-</sup> is then acidified with H<sup>+</sup> to give RCOOH.
> 
> Step 4 uses LiAlH<sub>4</sub> in dry ether to reduce the carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Benzocaine is an ester based compound that is used medicinally as a local anaesthetic in pain relievers and cough drops. One of the first industrial processes to manufacture benzocaine was the five-step reaction shown in Fig. 1.1.

Fig. 1.2 shows an alternative reaction scheme for the production of benzocaine.

![Alternative reaction scheme for benzocaine production via Friedel-Crafts acylation followed by nitration, esterification, and reduction](assets/046-alternative-reaction-scheme-for-benzocaine-produ.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

i) Suggest why this reaction scheme is an improvement.

[1]

ii) Suggest why this reaction scheme may not work.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) This reaction scheme is an improvement because:
> 
> - There are fewer steps in the reaction scheme **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) This reaction scheme may not work because:
> 
> - The nitration of benzoyl chloride does not preferentially form 4-nitrobenzoyl chloride / nitration does not occur at carbon-4 of the benzene ring **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Chemists aim to minimise the number of steps in any reaction scheme as this improves efficiency and overall atom economy.
> 
> The key difference between the two schemes is in the first two steps. Fig. 1.1 uses methylation then nitration; Fig. 1.2 uses acylation then nitration.
> 
> Fig. 1.1 converts 4-nitromethylbenzene to 4-nitrobenzoic acid (an extra oxidation step). Fig. 1.2 avoids this by starting with Friedel-Crafts acylation.
> 
> However, the acyl chloride group in benzoyl chloride is an electron-withdrawing meta-director. Nitration of benzoyl chloride preferentially places the nitro group at carbon-3, not carbon-4. This gives 3-nitrobenzoyl chloride, which would produce the wrong isomer of benzocaine.

Ethene is used in the radical-free synthesis of 1-aminopropane as shown.

ethene $\overset{\mathrm{step}1}{\rightarrow}$ compound **A** $\overset{\mathrm{step}2}{\rightarrow}$ compound **B** $\overset{\mathrm{step}3}{\rightarrow}$ propylamine

Identify which step of the reaction scheme could use potassium cyanide dissolved in ethanol. Explain your answer.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The step that could use potassium cyanide / KCN dissolved in ethanol is step 2. Marks are only awarded if step 2 is correctly identified.
> 
> - It cannot be step 1 because the cyanide ion / CN<sup>-</sup> is a nucleophile
> **AND**
> It will not react with / attack the C=C double bond of ethene **[1 mark]**
> - It cannot be step 3 because the reaction of CN<sup>-</sup> / KCN with compound **B** does not produce an amine
> **AND**
> A reduction step is required to convert the nitrile group to an amine **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> There are three steps and two marks, which combined with 'explain your answer' suggest that you should gain marks for explaining why two steps cannot use potassium cyanide.
> 
> Potassium cyanide provides CN<sup>-</sup> ions, which act as nucleophiles. Nucleophiles attack electron-deficient centres (positive or partial positive carbons), not electron-rich C=C double bonds.
> 
> Step 2 is a nucleophilic substitution: the CN<sup>-</sup> ion displaces the halide from compound **A** (a haloalkane), extending the carbon chain by one to give compound **B** (a nitrile). This is why KCN in ethanol is the correct reagent rather than not HCN, which is used for nucleophilic addition to carbonyl groups.

**Extract:**

1-(3-aminophenyl)ethanol can be synthesised from benzene by the route shown in Fig. 5.1.

![Synthesis route for 1-(3-aminophenyl)ethanol from benzene via nitration, Friedel-Crafts acylation, and reduction steps](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2023/06/synthesis-of-1-3-aminophenylethanol.png)

Fig. 5.1

Compound A = nitrobenzene

Step 2, in Fig. 5.1 in part **(a)**, is the reaction of compound **A** with ethanoyl chloride, CH<sub>3</sub>COCl, in the presence of a suitable catalyst.

State the catalyst required for this reaction and write an equation to show how the catalyst forms the electrophile for this reaction.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The catalyst required for this reaction and the equation to show how the catalyst forms the electrophile are:
> 
> - Aluminium trichloride / AlCl<sub>3</sub>
> **AND**
> CH<sub>3</sub>COCl + AlCl<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> + AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is another example of an electrophilic substitution reaction, for which you could be asked to draw the mechanism.
> 
> You need to know the reagents and conditions for Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation.
> 
> Both reactions require an appropriate halogenoalkane or haloacyl compound and a halogen carrier catalyst such as AlCl<sub>3</sub>.
> 
> The halogen in the catalyst must match the halogen in the reacting molecule.
> 
> You should also be able to explain how the catalyst forms the electrophile.

**Extract:**

1-(3-aminophenyl)ethanol can be synthesised from benzene by the route shown in Fig. 5.1.

![Synthesis route for 1-(3-aminophenyl)ethanol from benzene via nitration, Friedel-Crafts acylation, and reduction steps](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2023/06/synthesis-of-1-3-aminophenylethanol.png)

**Fig. 5.1**

Step 3, in Fig. 5.1 in part **(a)**, is the reaction of compound **B** with tin and hydrochloric acid, converting a nitro group into an amino group.

State **two** changes that occur to compound **B** during this reaction to show that reduction has taken place.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Two changes that occur to compound **B** during this reaction to show that reduction has taken place are:
> 
> - Oxygen is lost
> **AND**
> Hydrogen is gained **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You do not need to know the structure of compound **B** to answer this question.
> 
> The key piece of information is that a nitro group, -NO<sub>2</sub>, is being converted into an amino group, -NH<sub>2</sub>.
> 
> Therefore, oxygen is being lost and hydrogen is being gained.
> 
> There is more than one way to describe reduction:
> 
> - Loss of oxygen
> - Gain of hydrogen
> - Gain of electrons

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

1-(3-aminophenyl)ethanol can be synthesised from benzene by the route shown in Fig. 5.1.

![Synthesis route for 1-(3-aminophenyl)ethanol from benzene via nitration, Friedel-Crafts acylation, and reduction steps](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2023/06/synthesis-of-1-3-aminophenylethanol.png)

{align=center} **Fig. 5.1**

Step 4, in Fig. 5.1 in part **(a)**, is the reduction of compound **C** to 1-(3-aminophenyl)ethanol using NaBH<sub>4</sub>.

The structure of 1-(3-aminophenyl)ethanol is repeated in Fig. 5.2.

![Skeletal structure of 1-(3-aminophenyl)ethanol showing the secondary alcohol and amino functional groups](assets/049-skeletal-structure-of-1-3-aminophenyl-ethanol-sh.png)

**Fig. 5.2**

i) Draw a circle around the aliphatic functional group that is formed **after** the reaction of compound **C** with NaBH<sub>4</sub>.

[1]

ii) Draw the structure of compound **C**.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
i) The aliphatic functional group formed after the reaction of compound **C** with NaBH<sub>4</sub> is:

![Structure of 1-(3-aminophenyl)ethanol with the secondary alcohol OH group circled](assets/050-structure-of-1-3-aminophenyl-ethanol-with-the-se.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the OH / hydroxyl group correctly identified

ii) The structure of compound **C** is:

![Skeletal structure of 1-(3-aminophenyl)ethan-1-one showing the ketone functional group](assets/051-skeletal-structure-of-1-3-aminophenyl-ethan-1-on.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct structure of compound **C** shown

> **[exam-tip]**
> NaBH<sub>4</sub> is a reducing agent used to reduce:
> 
> - Aldehydes to primary alcohols
> - Ketones to secondary alcohols
> 
> Since the product, 1-(3-aminophenyl)ethanol, contains a secondary alcohol group, compound **C** must be a ketone.
> 
> To deduce the structure of compound **C**:
> 
> - Remove the H from the C–OH group
> - Remove the H attached to the same carbon
> - Replace the C–OH single bond with a C=O double bond
